ideas.title: Custody Mutual: jail-health liability program priced on clinical process data
ideas.one_liner: An MGA-style insurance program for jails that prices and discounts coverage from a few clinical-process indicators in the medical vendor's record, and that covers the county when a bankrupt vendor's indemnity proves worthless.
ideas.customer: County governments, sheriffs and public-entity risk pools (about 3,000+ county jails; JCOIN counts 3,535).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: the county risk-management liability line or the pool's annual premium. Signer: county risk manager or administrator plus the board; for pools, the executive director and board.
ideas.problem: Jail-death suits now settle for $2.5M-$20M (Huerfano CO $9.19M, Cleveland OK $20M, Choctaw OK $4M). Cover is shrinking (an Oklahoma sheriff reports rates up as much as 300% in four years; one pool excluded its jail; a vendor cut its limit from $10M to $8M). A vendor's indemnity is a promise from the party most likely to be insolvent when the claim lands (Lane County OR had to file a claim in Wellpath's bankruptcy; YesCare liquidated May 2026). Counties cannot see the clinical data that predicts losses because it sits in the vendor's EHR.
ideas.solution: Excess and contractual-liability layers that respond when the vendor cannot pay; premium keyed to a short list of process indicators (time to receiving screen, withdrawal scoring, sick-call response time, medication-administration omissions for chronic meds, provider escalation, community-med continuity, cell-check logs) fed from the vendor or county EHR under contract language the county requires; monthly dashboards and quarterly nurse audits as loss control; premium credits for data sharing and hitting thresholds. Structure the analysis as privileged patient-safety work (PSO) so the data is not a deliberate-indifference exhibit.
ideas.why_now: Wellpath Chapter 11 (Nov 2024) and YesCare's liquidation (May 2026) just proved the indemnity gap in public; pools are excluding jails and cutting limits; verdicts and settlements keep rising; correctional EHR data is standardizing (NaphCare TechCare gets a NASPO vehicle Sept 16, 2026).
ideas.wedge: First product: 'indemnity-gap excess' for counties tied to Wellpath or YesCare (Lane OR has an open death suit and bankruptcy claim; Orange NY, Polk FL, Fayette and Louisville KY were YesCare customers), plus a free 'clinical autopsy' of five years of closed claims for 2-3 state county pools. First 10: two or three pools and six or seven counties of 500-2,000 ADP with $2M+ in jail losses.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: 1,200 jail deaths a year (BJS 2019) x 30-40% producing a claim x $2-3M all-in = $0.7-1.4B; add 50% for non-fatal neglect/injury claims = $1.1-2.2B annual loss cost; at 65-70% loss ratio that is $1.6-3.3B premium-equivalent, of which 40-60% is insurable rather than retained by self-insured counties = roughly $0.6-2.0B. $100M gross written premium is 5-15% share by year 5-6. Least certain sizing in the file; first-90-day test is pulling pool loss runs.
ideas.who_does_it_today: County risk pools (e.g. Maine's county Risk Pool, about $220k/yr liability for Somerset County), excess-and-surplus jail programs marketed by wholesalers, vendors' own professional-liability carriers (narrowing), brokers. Funded startups: none found for jail liability specifically (searched, may have missed one). Free substitute: taxpayer self-insurance.
ideas.why_they_lose: Pools are consensus-governed and price by headcount and claims history, so they cannot tell a good medical vendor from a bad one; carriers have no clinical data and exit after bad years; vendors cannot hand over data that would be used against them in discovery.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the only dataset linking clinical process indicators to claim outcomes across vendors) plus switching costs (data feeds written into contracts, premium credits); scale economies in reinsurance later.
ideas.earned_secret: Large jail losses are not random: a short list of process failures shows up in timestamps days before the death, and the county never sees it because the vendor holds the record. The insurer that can see it can price it. Also: indemnity from a thin-capital vendor is worth least exactly when it is needed.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign two pools or counties as design partners; run the clinical autopsy on 50 closed claims and test whether the indicators separate bad from average outcomes; pick a fronting carrier and reinsurer for the indemnity-gap layer; draft the data-feed rider; get counsel on PSO/privilege structure and HIPAA health-care-operations basis. Legal gates: punitive damages uninsurable, MGA/fronting rules, deliberate-indifference risk if data shows notice and nobody acts.

ideas.title: Outside Care Plan: the DOC's own off-site health plan
ideas.one_liner: A risk-bearing benefit manager that takes all off-site care (hospital, ED, specialty, dialysis, oncology) for a state DOC or large jail system at a fixed per-member-per-month price, with referral-timeline guarantees, Medicaid match capture and case management for the sickest 1-3%.
ideas.customer: State corrections departments (36 outsource at least part, 14 are in-house, per the pool file, unverified) and the largest county jail systems.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: the DOC's off-site/'outside medical' line, or the pass-through portion of a capitated vendor's contract. Signer: DOC commissioner or CFO with the health services director; legislature approves.
ideas.problem: Off-site care is 20-27% of prison health budgets (Virginia 27%, New York 23% in 2015; about 20% across ten states). It is paid at near-chargemaster rates with double and unbundled billing common (NCCHC). Under pure capitation the on-site vendor is both gatekeeper and payer, so delayed referrals are its profit and its lawsuit, and the state is closed off from savings (Pew). Hospitals are unpaid by failed vendors (750+ Georgia providers claiming $75.6M from Wellpath), degrading access. Medicaid inpatient exception is under-claimed (reported savings $2.8M-$19M per state).
ideas.solution: Per-member-per-month carve-out with Medicare-based network rates (federal precedent: Marshals Service repricing at Medicare), independent utilization review with published timelines (specialist in 14/30 days), eConsult to avoid trips (jail study: 20% of specialty cases handled on-site), Medicaid eligibility and inpatient claims for expansion adults, case management for the top 1-3% (dialysis, cancer, cirrhosis, dementia), and 15-day hospital payment which is what buys the discount.
ideas.why_now: Vendor failure turned off-site access into a visible crisis; emergency procurements (Georgia 2024, Alabama 2026) show states will restructure fast; Safety Net Connect's July 2025 correctional expansion shows the category waking up.
ideas.wedge: Shadow bid in one or two states with in-house or lightly capitated health and Medicaid expansion; also county systems with their own hospital contracts. First 10: three states and seven large counties.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: off-site is 20-27% of ~$11B = $2.2-3.0B for state prisons, plus perhaps $1B for jails. $100M of premium needs about $125M of today's off-site spend: one big state (North Carolina's whole prison health budget was $400M in FY2024) or three or four mid-size states; about 12-15 states have off-site lines that large. Premium is gross; expected margin 5-8% before reinsurance cost. Needs ~3-4% of the state-prison off-site pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Prime Health Services (shared-savings repricing for county sheriffs, $88M cumulative documented savings, no risk), Florida Sheriffs Association inmate medical cost program, CorrectCare Integrated Health (jail claims payer), HealthSmart (TPA), NaphCare (off-site management for the BOP), Safety Net Connect (eConsult), big vendors' own networks, Centurion's parent Centene (a Medicaid plan). Repricing alone is a small fee pool, so the idea only works as risk-bearing with access guarantees.
ideas.why_they_lose: Repricers earn only on savings and promise nothing on access; the on-site vendor is paid more when referrals are delayed; our per-member price is paid regardless of how many referrals are approved, so the saving comes from rates, not denial.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (hospital contracts improve with volume and contract term), counter-positioning (incumbent vendors cannot give up gatekeeping), process power (utilization review plus case management).
ideas.earned_secret: Hospitals will take Medicare-plus rates only if paid in 15 days and given stable volume for 5-10 years. A three-year capitated vendor can promise neither, so the DOC pays chargemaster. And the lawsuits come from the delayed referral, not from the price.
ideas.first_90_days: Public-records request for three years of off-site claims in three states; reprice at 140% of Medicare to size the gap; get one hospital system to sign a letter of intent; get a stop-loss quote and actuarial sizing; present shadow bids to DOC finance directors. Check whether a per-member service contract needs a TPA/health-plan license and which states have rate-cap statutes.

ideas.title: Clinical Corps: pre-cleared nurse and tele-psychiatry pool
ideas.one_liner: A W-2 pool of nurses and tele-psychiatry clinicians with standing security clearance and correctional training for a state's facilities, dispatched in 24-72 hours and billed per verified hour with a fill-or-credit guarantee, replacing registry and agency nursing.
ideas.customer: State DOCs with in-house health (North Carolina, South Dakota), the California mental health Receiver and CCHCS, plus vendors that subcontract overflow.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: agency/contract nursing and tele-mental-health lines. Signer: DOC deputy secretary for health or CFO; the Receiver's staff; a vendor's VP of operations.
ideas.problem: Nursing vacancy above 44% in North Carolina, LPN 53% and RN 40% in South Dakota, mental-health vacancy 29% in California (April 2024), Wellpath cited 40% turnover in Georgia. Contract nurses cost $64/hr vs $25.40 for state staff in NC. California counted $592M of savings from unfilled posts and does not track missed shift minimums. Generalist agencies cannot place a nurse into a prison in 24 hours because background checks, key control and PREA/security orientation take weeks.
ideas.solution: Recruit (including displaced Wellpath/YesCare staff: 119 laid off in Shelby, 100+ unpaid in Fayette), clear and train once per state, pay above state scale, rotate across 5-20 facilities, add virtual nursing and tele-psychiatry under licensure compacts, verify hours by badge so the buyer pays only for filled shifts.
ideas.why_now: Published vacancy crises; a court-appointed mental health Receiver (effective Sept 1, 2025) with authority to contract outside civil-service pay scales; the LAO recommends allowing out-of-state tele-mental-health providers; a pool of experienced correctional nurses suddenly between employers. Pattern transferred: Timee's instant-pay spot labor in a shortage economy x Mercor's vetted-expert network; it has not happened because the scarce thing in prisons is a cleared nurse, not a licensed one.
ideas.wedge: Two states with published crises (North Carolina, South Dakota): pilot 10 FTE-equivalents at ~$54/hr vs $64; then the California Receiver's tele-psychiatry gap; then vendors' overflow. First 10: five DOCs, the Receiver, four vendors.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: if agency/contract labor is 8-12% of state-prison health budgets (South Dakota's travel-nurse spend is 12% of its clinical budget request), that is $0.9-1.3B a year, plus jails and vendor overflow. $100M of revenue is 8-11% of the state-prison slice (e.g. 15-20 states at $5-7M). Gross margin typical of staffing, 20-25%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: AMN, Cross Country, Aya and other travel-nurse firms (corrections share unverified); vendors' own recruiters; per-diem marketplaces such as ShiftKey and Clipboard Health (corrections share unverified); a Sourcewell staffing contract that lists clinical staffing; CFG's CareLink telehealth (Feb 2026); overtime and state float pools as the free substitute.
ideas.why_they_lose: Generalist agencies will not pre-clear and train per state; vendors cannot pay above their per-diem; states are held by civil-service pay scales and pay 2.5x through agencies instead.
ideas.moat: Weak: switching costs and process power from standing clearances and a correctional-ready credential, plus scale economies in credentialing. A rival can copy it in 6-12 months.
ideas.earned_secret: The scarce asset is a cleared, trained, willing correctional nurse. Whoever holds the pool of already-cleared nurses owns the only scalable supply, and states lose a month every time they onboard.
ideas.first_90_days: Clear 40 nurses in one state, sign a pilot priced per verified hour, resolve compact-state licensure, and call the Receiver's office and the LAO analyst about tele-mental-health pilots. Check W-2 vs 1099, staffing-agency licensing and civil-service contracting-out rules.

ideas.title: Piggyback Prime: the first cooperative contract for jail medical services
ideas.one_liner: Win a cooperative-purchasing master agreement (or a large state contract with a political-subdivision piggyback clause) for jail medical services so any county can join in days, with uniform quality standards, a pooled insurance/indemnity backstop, and regional operators or public hospitals delivering care.
ideas.customer: Counties and states that need a vendor fast after a failure, and mid-size counties with a single bidder.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: the county jail-medical line via a participating addendum. Signer: county administrator and sheriff.
ideas.problem: Replacement takes roughly 9-12 months of RFP while failure takes days; Georgia (2024) and Alabama (2026) both sole-sourced in emergencies and a losing vendor sued over Georgia's; counties with one bidder have no leverage; thin-balance-sheet vendors cannot back their indemnities.
ideas.solution: The prime holds the master agreement, rate card, SLAs and the insurance (via a captive or the Custody Mutual program); it subcontracts delivery to regional operators, public hospital systems or Clinical Corps clinicians; counties get one accountable party and a switching clause.
ideas.why_now: The 2024-26 failure wave (Wellpath, YesCare, Shelby exit, Alabama's ~$1B contract) and NaphCare's TechCare EHR winning a NASPO ValuePoint vehicle (usable Sept 16, 2026) show buyers will use cooperative vehicles in this sector. Pattern transferred: Carahsoft's contract-vehicle wrapper on pass-through flows; it has not happened because sheriffs buy county by county and operators are rivals, not subcontractors.
ideas.wedge: Win one lead-agency award or a state contract with a piggyback clause, then recruit counties with expiring contracts. First 10: a lead agency and nine counties.
ideas.path_to_100m: Gross: 6-10 mid-size county contracts at $10-19M each (Placer ~$18.7M/yr, Monterey ~$14.8M/yr by my arithmetic), or one mid-size state. Net: a prime keeps perhaps 8-12%, so $100M gross is $8-12M net. $100M net would need roughly $1B gross, about 20% of an estimated $5B jail pool: heroic. Treat as a $100M-gross business only.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody found for care delivery: my search found cooperative contracts for jail supplies (NASPO, OMNIA), corrections products (Sourcewell), generic clinical staffing (Sourcewell 061324-INF) and an EHR (TechCare), but none for medical services (may have missed one). Counties' bespoke RFPs and emergency procurements are the incumbent process; NaphCare could extend its vehicle.
ideas.why_they_lose: Operators will not subcontract to a rival; cooperatives prefer clean product catalogs over professional-services liability; sheriffs fear losing local control.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the master agreement itself, which requires winning a competitive solicitation) plus scale economies in pooled risk. Thin.
ideas.earned_secret: Emergency procurements are the real purchasing event in this industry, and they go to whoever is already on paper with ready capacity, not to the best bidder.
ideas.first_90_days: Read the cooperatives' solicitation calendars; ask Sourcewell, NASPO and OMNIA whether a services solicitation exists or is planned; draft a rate card from published awards (Placer, Monterey, Maryland); sign two regional operators as conditional subcontractors. Check each state's procurement code on piggybacking for clinical services and prime licensure.

ideas.title: Day 91: reentry care organization that starts inside the walls
ideas.one_liner: A reentry care organization that works inside facilities for the 90 days before release (paid by Medicaid under 1115 waivers), then holds a per-member contract with Medicaid plans for the first year after release, using a nurse, prescriber and community-health-worker team.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid agencies and Medicaid plans (Centene, Molina and others); DOCs and large jails are the access partners, not the payer.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: the 1115 pre-release benefit and targeted case management (state Medicaid director) and the plan's complex-care/enhanced-care-management budget (plan VP of complex care). Wrong-payer warning: a Connecticut study found the savings landed in the justice budget, not Medicaid, so the contract must be paid by the Medicaid benefit itself or share justice savings.
ideas.problem: Medicaid coverage in the month of release was 39% before a Wisconsin enrollment program; recently released people with chronic conditions cost Medicaid $1,356-$1,737 a month; the post-release period is the highest-risk window for overdose and death. Custody-health vendors are paid by the inmate-day inside the walls, plans cannot get inside and do not learn a release date until an ER visit, and community providers have no clearance and cannot bill.
ideas.solution: In-reach teams inside facilities, eligibility reactivation, a 30-day medication bridge in hand at the gate, MOUD/long-acting injectable continuity, an appointment within seven days, a 12-month community care team, and a release-date data feed from the DOC.
ideas.why_now: 19 states have approved reentry 1115 waivers; California is live statewide by Oct 1, 2026 (first-year: 42,000+ eligible, 160,554 claims); Washington runs it through plans; New Mexico's Just Health Plus pilot started July 2025; Louisiana treats plans as central. First time Medicaid pays for anything inside custody except hospital stays.
ideas.wedge: New Mexico, Washington or Louisiana, where plans are central: one plan plus one DOC or large jail. First 10: two plans, three DOCs, five large jails.
ideas.path_to_100m: The pre-release benefit alone is too small: California reimbursed only $16M to facilities in year one. The business must reach post-release. My arithmetic: care management at $200-300 PMPM for 12 months is ~$3,000 a person, so 33,000 members a year is $100M, about 7% of an estimated 500,000 high-need releases a year in expansion states (state-prison releases ~400,000 plus a share of millions of jail releases, 15% high-need assumed). Under full risk at $16-20k a member-year, about 5,000-6,000 members.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Wellpath, NaphCare and CFG reentry offerings; Transitions Clinic Network (nonprofit); Safety Net Connect's Collaborate platform; HealthTap with NaphCare for halfway-house patients; Reconnect ($3.3M raised, unverified) and Total Reentry Solutions (pre-seed, unverified); plans' in-house teams. My search did not confirm reentry work by Cityblock, Waymark or Pair Team.
ideas.why_they_lose: None combines facility access and security clearance, Medicaid billing and a risk contract: vendors are paid in-custody days, plans are blind to release dates, community organizations are non-clinical and cannot bill.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (facility access agreements and the release-date data feed), process power (in-reach protocol improving with each cohort), switching costs with DOCs.
ideas.earned_secret: The DOC knows the release date months ahead; the Medicaid plan finds out in the emergency room. Whoever owns the release-date pipe owns the cohort. (Pattern analog: Monogram/Cityblock risk-bearing care for a hidden high-need cohort.)
ideas.first_90_days: Pick one state; meet the Medicaid agency and one plan; obtain a data-sharing agreement for 24 months of release and claims history; price a PMPM from real claims; find a DOC or jail to host a 50-person pilot. Risks: federal Medicaid cuts and work requirements from 2027, waivers can be rescinded.

ideas.title: Cure Carve-Out: high-cost drugs out of the per-diem
ideas.one_liner: Take hepatitis C cure, HIV, long-acting MOUD and later GLP-1 drugs out of the capitated per-diem and run them as a funded program (testing, treatment, pharmacy, cure verification, release continuity), paid by the state per cure or per patient-month with drugs at cost.
ideas.customer: State DOCs and big jails, especially those under settlements or consent decrees (Colorado, Indiana, Kentucky and others).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: a separate pharmaceutical/program line. Signer: DOC medical director and CFO; legislature (the pending Cure Hepatitis C Act of 2026, HR 9682, would add subscription purchasing and grants but is not law).
ideas.problem: A capitated vendor pays each hepatitis C cure ($12-24k) out of its margin, so it rations and courts mostly side with patients: states treated under 1% of known infected inmates in 2015; Kentucky treated 159 of 1,670; New Mexico 123 of about 2,800; hundreds untreated in Mississippi under a $357M three-year VitalCore contract. Opt-out testing at intake is rare.
ideas.solution: Opt-out testing, test-and-treat, drug supply through a 340B partner or manufacturer subscription, adherence support, cure verification and handoff at release; the same chassis later covers HIV and long-acting buprenorphine.
ideas.why_now: Courts keep ruling for patients; cure prices fell to roughly $20k or less (Colorado 2024 settlement); federal subscription legislation is pending; opioid settlement terms list correctional MOUD as an allowed use.
ideas.wedge: A state under a hepatitis C settlement. First 10: four such states and six large jails.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: if 100,000-170,000 prisoners are infected (KFF Health News cites 1 in 7; base unverified) at $12-20k net that is $1.2-3.4B one-time, or $250-700M a year over five years; HIV (15-20k patients at ~$30k) adds $450-600M a year and long-acting MOUD at 10% of ~200,000 people with OUD about $420M a year. $100M gross is 6-10% of the ~$1-1.7B annual drug flow, but the operator's net fee would be 6-10% of that. Mostly pass-through, finite for hepatitis C; probably a feature of the Outside Care Plan rather than a company.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Vendors' own pharmacies and PBM relationships (ownership and markups not verified), manufacturer-direct deals (unverified), state programs treating in-house. No funded startup found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each cure costs them the margin on several hundred patient-months, so they cannot offer pass-through without giving up margin.
ideas.moat: Weak: scale in subscription and 340B purchasing, counter-positioning; replaceable by vendors once a state mandates a pass-through clause.
ideas.earned_secret: The litigation exposure from rationing a $20k cure exceeds the cost of the cure, and the capitation contract hides that from both sides until a judge shows up.
ideas.first_90_days: Read the Colorado, Indiana and Kentucky orders; price a test-and-treat program per cure; line up a 340B hospital partner and pharmacy license; ask Washington and Louisiana for subscription terms. Check HRSA 340B patient-definition rules for people in custody.

ideas.title: Day 21: forensic capacity for court-ordered competency restoration
ideas.one_liner: Secure psychiatric capacity that can come online in 6-12 months (jail-based restoration units and modular/converted licensed units), paid per bed-day by the state at 30-45% below a state hospital bed, with an outpatient track for low-risk defendants.
ideas.customer: State health agencies (Texas HHSC, Colorado CDHS, Washington DSHS, Oklahoma ODMHSAS) and host counties (Dallas County's sheriff has sued the state over 300+ detainees waiting more than 45 days).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: the state's forensic/private-bed contract line. Signer: HHSC deputy executive commissioner for state hospitals or the equivalent.
ideas.problem: About 1,700 people waited an average of six months in Texas jails; HHSC already contracts 747 private beds a day and 292 of its 2,770 beds were offline; Colorado's uncapped fines would have been $65.2M in FY24 (it paid the $12M cap); Washington has been issued $400M in fines and its new 350-bed hospital is not due until 2028. The sickest 5% of a jail consume its one-on-one watches, emergencies and lawsuits, and nobody owns the problem.
ideas.solution: License-ready modular units and jail-based programs staffed by Clinical Corps clinicians, on state contracts at roughly $380-450 per bed-day against about $500 for a state hospital bed (California 2012). Fines of $100-500 a day per waiting person mean a bed pays for itself when it opens.
ideas.why_now: A July 2026 federal injunction orders Texas to admit jailed incompetent defendants within 21 days (four years to comply); Colorado's decree expires in 2027 and it requests 94 new beds; Oklahoma paid $928,400 in fines in one month; state build timelines run years.
ideas.wedge: A 40-bed jail-based unit in a Texas county already suing the state, then a second Texas county, then Colorado's 94-bed request. First 10: three states and seven counties.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: $100M is about 600 beds at $450/day. Texas alone needs perhaps 600-1,000 more beds than the state is building (my estimate; no HHSC number found) worth $100-165M a year; Colorado's 94 beds are about $15M; Washington's 350-bed need about $55-60M if any is contracted. Nationally perhaps 3,000-4,000 unmet beds, so $100M is a 15-20% share.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Texas's private-bed vendors (unnamed in my sources), Wellpath Recovery Solutions and its Early Access and Stabilization program with California DSH, Liberty Healthcare (San Bernardino jail-based program, 96 beds, $17.98M over three years), and likely GEO Care, Universal Health Services and Acadia (unverified). Expect incumbents to bid.
ideas.why_they_lose: Hospital builders take years and rely on civil-service staff; incumbents' beds are tied up; a 6-12 month deployable unit beats a 2028 hospital.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (licensed and permitted beds, county site agreements) with some switching costs on 3-5 year contracts; the thinnest moat among the shock ideas. Pattern analog: policy money flows first to whoever holds permitted physical capacity (GEO/CoreCivic).
ideas.earned_secret: The people waiting 200+ days for a state bed are the most expensive and most dangerous patients in a county jail; the county pays for the jail while the state pays the fine, so a bed priced below the fine schedule is free money for the state.
ideas.first_90_days: Call the Dallas County sheriff's office; read the injunction's benchmark plan; pre-file for a state license for a 40-bed unit; get a staffing commitment from a Clinical Corps pilot. Check state hospital licensure and certificate-of-need rules, HHSC sole-source authority and county consent.

ideas.title: Open-Book Health Authority: fee-only management for counties that lost their vendor
ideas.one_liner: A fee-only management company that runs jail health as a county or public-hospital health authority: the county is employer and licensee, the company supplies leadership, recruiting backfill, pharmacy purchasing, EHR, telehealth, quality dashboards and Medicaid billing, and all costs are open-book.
ideas.customer: Counties and sheriffs with 300+ ADP that have lost or want to leave a vendor; public hospital districts and community health centers that want to run it but lack correctional know-how.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Payer: the county jail-medical line. Signer: county executive or administrator with the sheriff and board.
ideas.problem: A fixed per-diem pays the vendor for vacancies and denials; the county cannot verify staffing; failures end in emergency procurements. The costs the contract does not show (vacancy-driven agency labor, deputies on hospital watch at overtime, liability) land on the county.
ideas.solution: A management agreement with a fixed fee plus a capped at-risk portion tied to measured outcomes (access times, medication continuity, deaths per 1,000, vacancy), pass-through costs, and savings kept by the county. Clinicians are county or hospital employees, which helps with pensions and possibly Medicaid and 340B eligibility.
ideas.why_now: Vendor collapse created a new buyer behavior: Barnstable County MA moved in-house in 2023 after its vendor could not meet staffing; Wellpath is leaving Shelby County TN (119 jobs, Sept 30, 2026; AI-assisted source); Monterey and Placer switched vendors; YesCare's customers (about 20,000 people a day) scrambled in May 2026.
ideas.wedge: A 60-90 day emergency management bridge for a county whose vendor just failed, converting to a three-year agreement, with Clinical Corps providing backfill. First 10: five bridge customers and five conversions.
ideas.path_to_100m: Gross, including employer-of-record payroll: 6-10 county jails at $10-19M each (Placer ~$18.7M/yr, Monterey ~$14.8M/yr by my arithmetic) is $100-180M. The net management fee is 6-10% of that ($8-15M). $100M net would need the platform to add data/software revenue (Custody Mutual data, Outside Care Plan claims) or a state contract.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Hospital-run jail health systems (Cook County Health, NYC H+H and similar, from background knowledge, unverified), academic partners (UTMB and others, unverified), county in-house teams (Barnstable), consultants and RFP advisers. No vendor found selling a true fee-only ASO.
ideas.why_they_lose: Incumbents' profit is the spread between the per-diem and the cost (vacancies, denials, fewer hospital trips), so they cannot sell management without selling that spread; public hospitals cannot scale across counties.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning plus switching costs (county records and processes move onto the platform); weak on scale.
ideas.earned_secret: A jail's biggest health costs are the ones the contract does not show: the vendor profits from vacancies, while the sheriff pays for hospital watches and the county pays for liability.
ideas.first_90_days: Build a one-page open-book fee proposal from Placer and Monterey published contract values; interview the Barnstable sheriff and finance team; line up two public-hospital partners; check county employment, pension and sovereign-immunity rules in two target states, and Medicaid/340B eligibility of a county-employed clinic.

ideas.title: Second Look: independent per-case SNAP accuracy layer
ideas.one_liner: Recompute every SNAP certification before benefits issue, sample the caseload the way a federal re-reviewer does, and hand the state an audit-grade evidence trail, priced per case with a refund guarantee.
ideas.customer: State SNAP directors and human-services CFOs in states between the 6% and ~13% error tiers, starting with the five that lost delay eligibility (FL, MD, MA, NJ, NY), plus KS, VA, LA and large county operators. First 10: those five states, three large counties, two mid-size states.
ideas.payer_and_signer: State human-services commissioner plus budget director; budget lines are the SNAP payment-accuracy/QC unit and the new state-only benefit cost share from FY2028 (state general fund, so federal cost principles do not bind). SNAP director signs, CFO moves the money. About $25-35 per case-year, fixed, refund if audited correction rate misses target. Never contingent on the official QC rate.
ideas.problem: From FY2028 a state pays 0/5/10/15% of SNAP benefits by error tier (S). FY2025 national rate 10.62% = $10.1B improper; 41 states + DC are above 6%; CBPP/FFIS put the shift at ~$9.0-9.4B a year (CA $1.9B, FL ~$0.9B). The tier is set by a sampled statistic, so a state at a true 9.4% can land in the 15% tier by luck. Wages are the biggest error element (34-59% of error dollars in two state reports). OIG found consultants who 'eliminated errors' with unwarranted gains and USDA is reviewing those contracts, so states cannot prove an improvement is real.
ideas.solution: (1) Pre-issuance recompute on every certification, recert and interim report from the case file plus third-party wage, shelter and household data. (2) Shadow QC: replicate the FNS re-review protocol on a sample 10-50x the state's own, with confidence intervals, so the state knows which side of 6/8/10 it sits on in real time. (3) Immutable evidence ledger of what was known when and what was corrected, designed with an FNS regional office. (4) Worker-level coaching analytics. Later: Medicaid PERM eligibility audit-readiness (existing 3% recoupment, waivers narrowed about 2030), child-care and UI integrity.
ideas.why_now: FY2027's sample year began 2026-10-01 and, under the third-preceding-year rule, sets the FY2030 share (A); FY2026 closed 9/30 and FY2028 may use FY2025 or FY2026. Five states lost their delay exemption. Senate S.5526 (not law) would let the first year use the lower of FY2026/FY2027. SNAP admin became 75% state-funded on 2026-10-01.
ideas.wedge: Wage-income recompute on earned-income cases in two or three states; free shadow QC on 400 closed cases for each of the five lost-delay states; one paid county pilot ($250-400k).
ideas.path_to_100m: (U) ~22M SNAP households x $30 = ~$660M pool (A); $100M = 3.3M household-years = 15% of pool. Cross-check by exposure: $9.0-9.4B x 4-7% price-to-exposure = $360-660M, so 15-28% share. 3-5 big states do it (CA's $1.9B exposure alone supports $76-133M at 4-7%). Heroic only if states pay under 4% of exposure.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Deloitte (SNAP payment accuracy, 25+ states, self-reported reductions up to 35%), Public Consulting Group (SNAP accuracy improvement; the Wisconsin contingency deal), Human Services Group (Kansas since Oct 2025), Code for America, state QC units, FNS/APHSA technical assistance. No per-case independent assurance product found (light check).
ideas.why_they_lose: Deloitte and PCG sell hours, often build the systems they would audit, and cannot take a contingency without recreating the Wisconsin problem (PCG's 15% of a USDA bonus drew a DOJ probe). Self-reported improvement is unbankable after the OIG finding. Independence plus ledger plus refund guarantee cannot be copied without cannibalising consulting.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (independent, fixed price vs hourly consultants who also build the systems) + cornered resource (labelled corpus of FNS re-review findings across states) + process power.
ideas.earned_secret: QC's 'truth' is only what a federal reviewer can reproduce from third-party evidence for the sample month, so most error dollars (wages) are discoverable at certification time with the same sources. States skip universal queries because per-hit income-data prices keep rising (69-126% in four states over four years). Liability is a cliff on a noisy sample, so measuring the true rate is worth as much as lowering it. The safe fee is per case, never a share of the measured rate.
ideas.first_90_days: Pull FNS FY2025 state tables and public state QC reports; build an error-element model for three states; send the five lost-delay SNAP directors a free shadow-QC offer; get an FNS regional office to review the ledger design; close one county pilot; secure a design-partner state letter of intent.

ideas.title: Medicaid-Pending Bridge for nursing homes
ideas.one_liner: File every Medicaid long-term-care application in the admission month, assemble the five-year evidence file in parallel, and optionally advance cash against the pending receivable so operators stop carrying pending residents as free loans.
ideas.customer: Revenue-cycle leaders at nursing-home and assisted-living operators with high Medicaid mix (chains and large regionals). First 10: operators with 20-100 facilities in slow-processing states.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Operator CFO or VP revenue cycle. Budget: business-office labor, outsourced eligibility contingency fees (an existing line) and bad-debt write-offs. $750-1,250 per filed-and-approved application (A) plus a financing spread.
ideas.problem: From 2027-01-01 nursing-home applicants get at most two months of retroactive coverage (S). Coverage still starts in the application month, so the exposure is filing delay; families need five years of bank records and weeks to assemble them (S). Medicaid pays for over 60% of residents and LeadingAge warns providers may limit admission of Medicaid-pending residents (S).
ideas.solution: Day-one skeleton filing; consented bank connections and document capture; automated 60-month transfer screen with penalty-period modelling and a cure playbook (return of funds, exempt transfers) with partner elder-law attorneys; state-specific packet generator; up to 80% advance against expected Medicaid receivables priced on approval probability.
ideas.why_now: Retro cut starts 2027-01-01; operators will tighten admissions of pending residents, turning a process gap into a cash gap.
ideas.wedge: Ten facilities of one chain in two states; filing-in-month plus evidence packet only; add financing after 90 days of approval data.
ideas.path_to_100m: (U) ~1.2M nursing-home residents; (A) 600-800k new Medicaid LTC applications a year (nursing facility plus waiver programs). At $750-1,250 the pool is $450M-1B; $100M = 100-130k applications = ~15% share. Financing alternative: $0.6-0.8B average advances at 12-15% = $75-100M. Volume numbers are unverified and must be checked first.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Regional eligibility specialists and elder-law firms (U), chains' in-house business offices (U), hospital-oriented eligibility vendors extending into LTC (trade press names Change Healthcare, now Optum; old), bank-statement analytics such as Ocrolus which started on Medicaid eligibility in 2018. Competitor check was one search only.
ideas.why_they_lose: Contingency vendors are paid on approval and work in batches; none sells filing-in-month certainty plus bridge financing; in-house offices are labour-bound and turn over; attorneys price at a family level.
ideas.moat: Process power in state-specific rules + cost-of-capital edge + switching costs once embedded in the admissions workflow.
ideas.earned_secret: The retro cut does not move the coverage start date; it makes the application month the only variable that matters, so the process to optimise is time-to-filing, not time-to-approval. Denials and long pends come mostly from unexplained transfers in the look-back, not income; a transfer narrative prepared before the caseworker's first request is what shortens the process (U). The real asset is a state-by-state map of what triggers a pend letter.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 15 LTC eligibility supervisors and business-office directors; build five states' checklists; run 50 live filings with a design-partner chain; line up one elder-law partner; test price.

ideas.title: Continuity Manager: PMPM carve-out for the top Medicaid plans
ideas.one_liner: A coverage-continuity carve-out that plans buy per member per month, the way they buy transportation and dental managers, covering outreach, evidence assembly, cure tracking and reinstatement for expansion adults, firewalled from eligibility determination.
ideas.customer: COO, growth and chief medical officers at Centene (17.9% share), Elevance (10.6%), UnitedHealthcare (8.4%), Molina (6.0%) and CVS/Aetna; the Big Five hold about half of managed Medicaid. First 10: about ten state markets across three plans.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Plan COO/CFO. Budget: administrative load already in capitation rates plus member-engagement/retention. $1.25-2.50 PMPM on subject expansion adults, about $30 per member-year (A, 0.4% of a $7k capitation).
ideas.problem: Loss is mostly procedural (71% of unwinding disenrollments). Manatt projects 8.2M average annual losses (CMS: 2.3M in FY2027). Plans may only 'support': section 438.58 bars MCOs and affiliated entities from determining compliance. A plan that funds retention captures only part of the gain because retained members can re-enrol elsewhere after a lapse, so every plan under-invests (A).
ideas.solution: A delegated-entity service structurally independent of plan affiliates: ingest plan data (claims, pharmacy, ADT, care-management contacts, address changes) as supporting evidence under member consent; contact members on plan-permitted channels; pre-fill and submit as authorised representative where the state allows; run the 30-day cure clock; manage reinstatement within the reconsideration window (U, 90 days under 42 CFR 435.916) and hearings; report outcomes only; no determinations. Later a cross-plan statewide utility funded pro rata.
ideas.why_now: Start 2027-01-01 and semiannual renewals from July 2027; managed Medicaid already down 3.1M year on year (60.4M); acuity squeezed margins (Centene 9-month 2024 Medicaid margin -27%); Elevance says subject members are ~20% of its Medicaid book; Centene exits Arkansas expansion in 2027. Not done yet because plans had no forcing event, unwinding outreach was state-led and the plan-state firewall needs legal design.
ideas.wedge: One plan in one state with an early requirement (Georgia) plus one plan running six-month-renewal pilots elsewhere; sell on cost per retained member.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) ~16M expansion adults in managed care (20M x 80%) x $30 = $480M pool; $100M = 21% share (heroic). Alternatively 0.2-0.6% of the $16-57B of capitation revenue at risk (CMS vs Manatt x $7k). Five buyers, so five enterprise sales.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Fortuna Health (a16z; $18-22M reported, figures conflict; Unite Us partnership; sells to plans, providers and states), Unite Us, Reema Health ($7.6M), plans' in-house engagement teams, Maximus/Conduent outreach on state contracts, Propel on the SNAP side. Nobody found offering a PMPM-priced accountable carve-out.
ideas.why_they_lose: Fortuna sells software and engagement, not a risk-bearing PMPM service; Maximus and Conduent are paid by states and cannot sit on the plan side; plans cannot coordinate with each other or the state without a neutral party.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (embedded in plan data flows) + scale economies (50-state compliance map) + network effects (cross-plan utility).
ideas.earned_secret: The plan's best asset, member-level claims and contact data, is exactly the evidence the IFR names as ex parte sources, but plans may not determine anything, so the winning design ships evidence packets under consent and leaves determination to the state. Retention carve-outs get bought like NEMT, not like software, and the free-rider problem means a neutral cross-plan utility beats any single plan's tool.
ideas.first_90_days: Pitch the three largest plans; commission a legal memo on section 438.58, marketing and inducement rules and authorised-representative rules in five states; sign one design-partner plan on a PMPM pilot covering 20,000 lives.

ideas.title: Hours Marketplace: verified shifts for the 80 hours
ideas.one_liner: A marketplace of 2-4 hour community-service shifts at pre-vetted public and nonprofit hosts with instant verified hours delivered to state and plan systems, funded by the plans and programs that lose money when an enrollee fails.
ideas.customer: Hosts (parks departments, school districts, food banks, hospital auxiliaries, faith networks) and enrollees who cannot reach 80 hours of work; buyers are plan community-engagement leads and state SNAP E&T directors. First 10 hosts: anchor food banks and cities in two states; first payers: two plans.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Plan member-engagement/value-added-services budget (state approval needed) and state SNAP E&T programs (50% federal reimbursement of non-federal spend, about $550M nationwide in 2022). Signer: plan COO or state E&T director.
ideas.problem: Community service is a statutory path and the rule is broad (42 CFR 435.552(b): unpaid, structured, public or nonprofit benefit; need not be voluntary; court-ordered counts). There is no registry of volunteer hours. In Georgia 42% of interested applicants never filed a report showing any qualifying hours and 19% of complete applications were denied for under 80 hours or weak verification. Existing tools verify hours but nobody supplies capacity.
ideas.solution: Hosts post shifts; members book by text; geo/QR check-in and check-out; hours post to a ledger with host attestations and go to the state or plan by API; no-show handling, host liability cover, referral to job training and E&T. Transfers the instant-pay spot-labor marketplace pattern (Timee) to compliance hours.
ideas.why_now: CE starts 2027-01-01 and self-attestation ends 2028-01-01. Not done yet: no forced demand existed, volunteer platforms serve volunteers not compliance, and Georgia's programme was too small to matter.
ideas.wedge: One metro, one plan: 50 hosts, 5,000 member-months a month; expand to SNAP-overlap members for E&T reimbursement.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) 20M subject adults; 12-15% need non-job hours = 2.4-3.0M; serve 0.3-0.45M member-years at $300-350 = $90-160M, i.e. 10-15% of that need. Capacity check: 0.3M x 80 hrs x 12 = ~290M hours a year vs (U) ~5B hours of formal US volunteering, about 6%. Host supervision must be in-kind because paid supervision would cost more than the fee. Needs real host capacity, the binding constraint.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Better Impact (verified hours sold to state Medicaid), Helper Helper, volunteer platforms such as Galaxy Digital and VolunteerMatch (U), Maximus tracking tool (free to clients), Deloitte hub, Fortuna + Unite Us (hour verification), SNAP E&T providers.
ideas.why_they_lose: Verification vendors sell attestation, not supply; volunteer platforms have no state-verified record; state-owned trackers cannot run a marketplace.
ideas.moat: Network economies (hosts x members) + cornered resource (anchor host contracts).
ideas.earned_secret: The scarce thing is host capacity, not software; friction is in the first hour (Georgia). Public hosts count under the rule and court-ordered hours count, so municipal anchors are available. Legal check before building: wage-and-hour and workers' compensation treatment of compelled service (U; workfare participants have been treated as employees in other programmes).
ideas.first_90_days: Map anchor hosts in two states; talk to three food-bank networks; commission a legal memo on FLSA and workers' comp; get one plan to fund 1,000 slots; ship a text-based MVP.

ideas.title: Open Verification Exchange with a cheapest-first router
ideas.one_liner: A router that sends each state income/hours verification to free and low-cost sources before The Work Number, backed by a non-exclusive payroll-data exchange that pays payroll providers a real revenue share.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid, SNAP, TANF and child-care agencies hit by Work Number price hikes (NC, KS, CO, CT, SD) and states shopping contractors (Missouri uses SteadyIQ, Equifax and ID.me).
ideas.payer_and_signer: State Medicaid director or human-services CIO/procurement chief. Budget: eligibility verification line (50% federal admin match; systems 75-90% where built into eligibility systems, U), today paid per transaction to Equifax.
ideas.problem: Equifax guided to ~$800M of government revenue in 2025 and grew low double digits; The Work Number holds 209M active records and about half of states use it; per-query hikes of 126% (CO), 120% (KS), 95% (NC), 69% (CT) over four years; alleged exclusive deals with ADP, Intuit, Walmart and Home Depot are in antitrust discovery. The IFR forces ex parte checks first, so volume rises.
ideas.solution: Phase 1: a savings-share router that queries NDNH, state UI wages and the CMS Hub first, then consented payroll/gig connections, then The Work Number last. Phase 2: a non-exclusive payroll exchange paying 30-40% of verification revenue to payroll vendors and employers, plus consented gig/1099 connections (Argyle, Truv, Pinwheel as suppliers, not rivals). Same API serves SNAP accuracy and renewals.
ideas.why_now: Court denied dismissal (Feb 2025) and ordered some VOIE terms rewritten; senators' investigation Feb 2026; Medicaid verification volume jumps in 2027.
ideas.wedge: Router sold to three states on shared savings; first customers are the states named in the senators' letter.
ideas.path_to_100m: At a 35% price discount, $100M revenue = $154M of Equifax-equivalent volume = ~19% of an $800M government book (A). Waterfall mechanics mean the exchange need not cover everyone: roughly a 60% hit rate on cheap sources cuts Work Number queries by more than half (A). Adjacent programmes (SNAP, UI, housing, income-driven loan repayment) lift the ceiling.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Equifax Workforce Solutions; Experian and TransUnion employer-verification products (U); Argyle, Truv, Pinwheel, Atomic (consented payroll); ID.me; SteadyIQ; Deloitte's free year-one hub; CMS Hub (student, veteran); free public NDNH and state UI wages (access terms U).
ideas.why_they_lose: Equifax cannot pay suppliers more without repricing its whole book (mortgage verification is its profit pool, U), cannot discount to states without inviting price-discrimination claims in a live antitrust case (A), and its data come from payroll contracts so it cannot reach gig and self-employed work. Deloitte's hub is free for one year, then lock-in.
ideas.moat: Network economies (two-sided data) + scale economies (connector fixed costs) + counter-positioning (revenue share Equifax cannot match).
ideas.earned_secret: Equifax's moat is contractual, not technical, and it is under legal challenge; and a router does not need coverage parity to win, only to answer the cheap-first fraction and take a share of the savings.
ideas.first_90_days: File public-records requests for five states' price histories; build the router on free sources only; sign one state on shared savings; meet five payroll providers not named in the complaint (status unchecked).

ideas.title: Renewal Autopilot priced per auto-completed case
ideas.one_liner: Run the new semiannual Medicaid renewal and the SNAP recertification as a managed service paid per case completed without a caseworker touch, so the vendor earns more only when the state's touch volume falls.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid and SNAP operations chiefs and county human-services directors. First 10: states with six-month renewals and ex parte rates under about 60% (U).
ideas.payer_and_signer: State Medicaid director / COO with the CFO. Budget: eligibility operations and vendor contracts (50% federal admin match). Staff still make every decision.
ideas.problem: Expansion adults must renew every six months from 2027, ex parte first. Maximus's own guidance ties growth to redetermination volume starting July 2027 ('building year', full run rate FY2028), so the incumbent's incentive points the other way. SNAP admin became 75% state-funded on 2026-10-01.
ideas.solution: Assemble data from every permissible source before the renewal date; send determination-support packets to state staff for approval; contact members only for the residual; track cures; pay per auto-completed renewal plus shared savings against an agreed baseline.
ideas.why_now: July 2027 redetermination start; SNAP admin cost shift; ex parte-first rule.
ideas.wedge: One state's renewal queue for SNAP plus Medicaid; pre-populated renewals first.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) 40M Medicaid renewals + ~15M SNAP recertifications = 55M a year; manual cost $30-100 vs ~$5 automated, a ~$55 saving. At $12 per auto-completed case, $100M = 8.3M cases = 30% of national volume at 50% auto-completion, or 50% of volume if paid only on lift above the state baseline. Weakest path together with the Rules Twin.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Maximus, Conduent (work-requirements suite), GDIT, Deloitte hub, Gainwell, Accenture, state staff.
ideas.why_they_lose: Their revenue grows with volume and staff-hours; a vendor that cuts touches shrinks their line, so none will take an outcome contract on reducing them. Their free-year pledges are land-grabs, not outcome contracts.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (outcome pricing vs volume-paid incumbents) + process power.
ideas.earned_secret: The incumbent's growth story is the number of redeterminations, so no incumbent will sign a contract that pays for fewer of them.
ideas.first_90_days: Collect ex parte rate and cost-per-renewal data from five states; build one pre-population pipeline; sign a pilot priced against a measured baseline.

ideas.title: Exemption Evidence Utility, starting with medical frailty
ideas.one_liner: The audited source for exemption evidence: version-controlled medical-frailty code sets, claims-based acuity scoring on the 12-month lookback, and a paid clinician channel for cases data cannot resolve.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid directors, MMIS and analytics leads, and plan compliance officers. First 10: six large-exposure states and four plans.
ideas.payer_and_signer: State Medicaid agency (admin match 50%, systems up to 75-90%, U) co-funded by plans; signer is the state Medicaid director with CMS advance-planning approval, and the plan's chief compliance officer.
ideas.problem: Under the IFR frailty needs a diagnosis plus functional impairment; code lists must be auditable and regularly revised; only 12 months of claims count; reverify every 12 months; self-attestation once per enrollment period from 2028; New Hampshire providers refused unpaid forms; Code for America calls frailty the largest exemption category with no good free data source. Manatt says the narrow frailty rules drive extra coverage loss.
ideas.solution: (1) Versioned code-set library with a clinical advisory panel; (2) acuity engine run inside the state's warehouse (claims, encounters, pharmacy, DME); (3) an explanation record per exemption for audit; (4) a clinician channel: short standard form plus telehealth functional assessment, paid per completion; (5) a 12-month reverification scheduler. Extend to caregiver, student, treatment-participation and veteran exemptions.
ideas.why_now: Start 2027-01-01; documentation tightens 2028; Emmy and the Federal Hub do not cover frailty; the definition is under litigation.
ideas.wedge: Code set plus scoring in three states already running claims analytics; clinician channel in the same states; one co-funding plan.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) 12% of 20M = 2.4M frailty claimants (CT estimate); 40-60% unresolved by claims = 1.0-1.4M x $45 per packet = $45-63M; licences $0.8-1.2M x 40 states = $32-48M; total $77-111M with near-total adoption, about 60% of the frailty workflow. Adding the other exemption categories (roughly 35-45% of subject adults, A) roughly doubles volume and brings the needed share to about 25-30%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: State analytics teams, MMIS vendors (Gainwell, Conduent), Optum, risk-grouper vendors (U), CHCS technical assistance; no audited frailty product found (light check).
ideas.why_they_lose: Integrators bundle 'claims match' as a feature but do not carry clinical governance; risk-grouper vendors skip the functional-impairment step; plans are barred from determining.
ideas.moat: Standard (audited code sets accepted in CMS audit) + cornered resource (clinician network) + switching costs.
ideas.earned_secret: Frailty is an audit problem, not a matching problem: CMS says lists must be auditable and weakly supported determinations can cost the state, so the winner sells defensibility, and the cheapest way to resolve the residual is to pay a clinician ten minutes, not to build a better algorithm.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit a five-clinician advisory panel (psychiatry, addiction medicine, internal medicine, rehab, disability); build a v1 code set mapped to the five statutory categories; test on public claims files; interview six state policy directors; draft advance-planning language.

ideas.title: Rules Twin: versioned rules and a caseload digital twin
ideas.one_liner: A machine-readable record of every Medicaid and SNAP rule, waiver and exemption by state and date, plus a digital twin that replays each state's de-identified caseload through a proposed rule to forecast churn and error before go-live.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid and SNAP policy and IT directors; plan strategy and finance teams; navigator networks; integrators as OEM. First 10: four states, three plans, two networks or integrators, one OEM.
ideas.payer_and_signer: State advance-planning budgets (testing and independent-verification lines, U) and plan actuarial/strategy budgets; signer is the state Medicaid IT director with CMS approval, or the plan's chief strategy officer.
ideas.problem: The IFR rewrote dozens of rules, 26 states are suing, the SNAP cost-share start may move, and waivers vary by state. Eligibility logic sits in proprietary rule engines changed by change order (U). Nobody can tell a legislature or court how many people a given rule version affects, and the IFR requires auditable code sets.
ideas.solution: Rules-as-code library with citations; digital twin using synthetic and de-identified households; regression tests against the production eligibility system; drift monitoring; code-set registry shared with the exemption utility.
ideas.why_now: IFR amendments, litigation and the pending SNAP delay bill make rule volatility the permanent condition; the auditable-list requirement is new.
ideas.wedge: Forecast and regression test for one state's CE release; sell the same forecast to its plans.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) 43 Medicaid states x $1.2M + 50 SNAP/TANF programs x $0.5M + 25 plans/systems x $0.6M + integrator OEM $15M = ~$107M, which needs about 70% of states. Weakest path; kill if four states will not share de-identified caseloads.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nava and PolicyEngine (nonprofit/open source, U), integrators' proprietary engines (Merative/Curam, Deloitte), Salesforce public-sector (U), forecasting consultancies (Manatt, Milliman, Mercer). Light competitor check only.
ideas.why_they_lose: Integrators earn on change orders and do not simulate against real caseloads; nonprofits lack procurement staying power and a paid data-sharing relationship.
ideas.moat: Process power + cornered resource (cross-state rule library and caseload models) + switching costs.
ideas.earned_secret: Integrators are paid to deliver to specification, not to ask what a specification does to a real caseload (U); the question the legislature and CMS now ask is exactly the twin's output.
ideas.first_90_days: Encode the CE rule as code with citations; run a synthetic-household test on one state's published rules; offer plans a free state-by-state forecast; line up one state data-sharing agreement.

ideas.title: Slot Book: block-booked engine shop capacity for mid-tier operators
ideas.one_liner: Sign take-or-pay capacity blocks at independent engine shops and resell guaranteed-window shop visits to the operators too small to command a slot.
ideas.customer: Mid-tier airlines (20-80 aircraft, mostly 737NG/A320ceo with some LEAP/GTF) and small lessors that queue behind LTSA customers and big lessors.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Airline engine-MRO budget line plus the engine-lease line that pays for cover engines during delays. Signer: VP Technical Operations or Director of Engine Asset Management (lessor: Head of Technical). Reservation fee (10-15% of expected visit value, assumption) escrowed at booking, balance at release.
ideas.problem: Capacity, not price, is the binding constraint. Bain: slot waits up 2-3 months (sometimes 6). Oliver Wyman: narrowbody turnaround regularly 180-200+ days, and over half of respondents expect no improvement within three years. IBA: short-term next-gen cover engines above $6,500 a day. Shops sell slots to whoever commits forecastable volume; a 30-aircraft airline's removals are lumpy, so it gets leftovers and pays twice (cover engine plus an extended lease; Willis says airlines sign ~3-year leases for shorter needs).
ideas.solution: A capacity book: 12-24 month take-or-pay blocks at 6-10 independent shops, resold as visit rights that are fungible across customers and workscopes inside the block (swap, defer, upgrade), with a guaranteed induction window, a kit-readiness plan and an optional pre-priced cover engine from partner lessors. Pooling ~100 operators turns lumpy demand into a smooth pipeline shops will discount for. Legal premise: contract capacity, not a licensed activity; operator keeps airworthiness responsibility, shop keeps its ratings; check take-or-pay exposure, assignment/subcontracting limits in OEM licenses (unverified) and buyer-pool antitrust (mild).
ideas.why_now: Capacity reservation just became the currency: StandardAero signed a capacity general terms agreement with lessor AviLease (Mar 2026) for LEAP and CFM56-7B. IATA/Emerton (Jun 2026) sees LEAP visits rising from 600-800 to 5,000+ and GTF from ~1,000 to 2,000+ by 2040; Bain expects demand to exceed supply ~17% through 2030; IndiGo reports LEAP overhauls at 230 days and GTF over 300.
ideas.wedge: CFM56-7B and -5B first: 40+ shops overhaul CFM56 and about two-thirds of visits are already outside CFM's own shops (GE Aerospace article), so counterparties are plentiful. First 10 customers: 737NG/A320ceo operators and small lessors in Latin America, Eastern Europe, India/Southeast Asia and Africa, served from a 60-visit pilot book at 2-3 second-tier shops (not StandardAero).
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumptions: ~4,700 narrowbody visits a year (GTF ~1,000 and LEAP 600-800 sourced; ~3,000 legacy is my estimate), average visit ~$4.5M, take ~4.5% (reservation spread plus 3-5% commission) = ~$200k per visit. $100M needs ~500 visits (~$2.25B booked) = ~11% of all narrowbody visits and ~26% of mid-tier visits (est. 40% of volume): heroic. It drops to ~8% of mid-tier slot-constrained spend (~$28B, estimate) only if the book also spans widebody/regional engines and airframe heavy-check, landing-gear and APU slots. Kill it if engine-only mid-tier share cannot reach ~15%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Lessor capacity agreements (StandardAero-AviLease); engine-management firms that run RFQs and monitor shops (AJW Group: shop control, work-scope designation, advance material purchasing; Acumen: engine management, invoice review, reserve-claim analysis); Sanad (end-to-end engine services plus asset management); Willis Lease (own module shop). Unverified: OEM LTSAs bundle slot priority for big customers. I found no neutral capacity aggregator for the mid-tier.
ideas.why_they_lose: Shops sell direct but dislike lumpy demand; engine-management firms are agents with no slot inventory or balance sheet; lessors only book capacity for their own assets; OEM LTSAs are bundled and not fungible across customers.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (portfolio smoothing earns better slot terms, which attracts more operators), counter-positioning against bundled LTSAs, and cornered resource in multi-year capacity blocks.
ideas.earned_secret: The scarce thing is a shop's ability to plan against a commitment, not the visit itself. Slots go to forecastable volume, and a small airline's contract turnaround remedies are weak, so it pays for delay twice. Pooled demand from ~100 such operators has statistical smoothness one operator cannot offer (insider hypothesis, unverified); lessors buying capacity agreements shows the same trade at the top.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 shop sales heads and planners; sign LOIs for ~30 CFM56-7B slots each at 3 shops on a take-or-pay discount; pre-sell 40 visit rights to 8 operators as paid reservations; model cancellation risk from 24 months of operator removal history.

ideas.title: The Repair Library: approved-repair IP for engine piece parts
ideas.one_liner: Own a library of FAA/EASA-approved repair schemes for engine piece parts, with field evidence behind each, and run automated repair cells that use it.
ideas.customer: Independent engine shops and lessor module shops (repair customers); lessors who can require approved schemes in workscope clauses.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Shops pay per repaired part (tolling) and royalties for licensed use. Signer: VP Engineering or VP Materials at the shop; for specification, the lessor's Head of Technical.
ideas.problem: Missing piece parts are the main cause of slow engine turnaround (Bain), and OEMs issue too few repair licenses. Whether a part is scrapped or repaired depends on whether an approved repair scheme exists for that damage, not on metallurgy. Schemes are OEM-owned or hoarded by one shop, so the same weld is re-qualified repeatedly. HEICO says its repair business is supply-constrained.
ideas.solution: (1) An approved-scheme library (14 CFR 43.13 and Part 21 major-repair data via DERs; EASA Part 21 Subpart M), starting with warm/cold-section CFM56-7B/-5B and V2500 parts with DER precedent. (2) Per-part royalties from licensed shops. (3) Own automated cells (laser cladding / directed-energy deposition, robotic blending) in 2-3 hubs, storing CT or flow-test data for every repaired part to build field evidence. Legal premise: major repair data must be approved; OEM manuals are proprietary so independent substantiation is required (FAA SAIB NE-13-33R2 on DER repairs of CFM56-5 nozzle segments shows the liability); export classification of engine technical data and OEM license terms need checking (unverified).
ideas.why_now: Bain names missing parts as the main turnaround driver; IATA asks for faster repair development and licensed production and renewed its CFM agreement in Jan 2026 covering regulator-approved non-OEM repairs; OEMs are racing in (Pratt's additive GTF repair cuts process time 60%+ and expects to recover $100M of parts over five years; GE Singapore is approved for additive component repair), which proves the economics.
ideas.wedge: 5 high-scrap, high-volume CFM56-7B parts with existing DER precedent; 2 independent shops as licensees. First 10 customers: second-tier CFM56 shops, lessor module shops and one airline in-house shop.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumptions (mine): engine MRO $50.7B (sourced) x ~55% materials = $28B; piece-part repair ~20% of materials = ~$5.6B; independent-addressable ~40% = ~$2.2B. Year-5 mix: own cells bill ~$65M (1.2% of $5.6B) plus royalties ~$35M (17.5% on ~$200M licensed repair value, 3.6% of $5.6B) = $100M. Licensing alone would need ~$570M of repair value (~26% of the independent-addressable pool), so the cells are required. Capital: 3 hubs at $25-40M (estimate); R&D ~150 schemes at ~$300k (estimate). Pratt's single additive program (~$20M a year of recovered parts) shows one scheme's scale; the model needs about five.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Chromalloy (DER repairs on CFM56 hot-section parts), GKN Aerospace (multi-year P&W repair contracts across 20+ component types), HEICO (repair, DER/PMA, Wencor), Jet Parts Engineering (PMA and DER, mostly outside the hot section), OEM programs (P&W additive, GE Singapore) and shops' in-house schemes.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs earn more on a new part than a repair; licensed shops will not license schemes to rivals; HEICO optimizes for PMA parts and its own capacity; a neutral library sees field data from every shop and becomes the standard no single shop can match.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (approved data plus the field-evidence database), process power (repair-cell know-how), switching costs (shop qualification).
ideas.earned_secret: Scrap vs repair is a paperwork fact (does an approved scheme exist?), not a physics fact. What regulators, lessors and insurers accept is field evidence, so the winner is whoever stores post-repair CT/flow data for every part. Insider hypothesis (unverified): scrap rates on high-value airfoils run in the tens of percent; the one source I found was paywalled, so verify in interviews.
ideas.first_90_days: Hire two DERs and a materials engineer; choose 5 parts using scrap data from 3 shops; run a 100-part pilot with CT/flow data; present results to 3 lessors and 2 shops; get one lessor to name approved schemes in a workscope clause.

ideas.title: Fleet Buying Group: a Vizient for aircraft maintenance with PMA offtake pools
ideas.one_liner: A vendor-paid buying group that pools mid-tier maintenance volume and uses it to fund PMA offtake for the part numbers nobody develops.
ideas.customer: Mid-tier airlines, small lessors and independent MROs buying parts, component repair, consumables and ground support.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Vendors pay admin fees (healthcare benchmark: Premier's suppliers pay 1-3% of purchase price) plus a member fee for benchmarking. Signers: VP Supply Chain or CFO at members; chief commercial officer at vendors.
ideas.problem: The mid-tier negotiates alone. Oliver Wyman: 2025 material inflation ran 100-200 bp above expectations, with more expected; ~90% of firms report tariff effects. Sole-source OEM prices reflect volume tier, not cost (unverified), and PMA developers choose part numbers by OEM price times visible volume, so scattered mid-tier volume is invisible and parts HEICO skips never get developed. Historic PMA share was only ~2-4% of parts deliveries (2006-2011 data).
ideas.solution: Year 1: private price benchmarks from members' PO data (top 200 part numbers). Year 2: pooled RFPs on rotables, expendables and component repair with rebates. Year 3: offtake letters that fund PMA/DER development for chosen part numbers, with savings shared. Maps to IATA's ask for predictable spare-part pricing. Legal premise: buyers' groups are usually judged under the rule of reason; unverified: FTC/DOJ withdrew their 2000 competitor-collaboration guidelines in Dec 2024 and the EU 2023 horizontal guidelines give a ~15% joint-purchasing safe harbor; the healthcare GPO safe harbor does not apply; vendor-paid fees need disclosure; OEM most-favored-customer clauses may limit discounts.
ideas.why_now: Material inflation and tariff exposure are rising; the Section 232 negotiation window ends ~Jan 5 2027; IATA made price transparency and non-OEM options a priority (CFM agreement renewed Jan 2026); HEICO is adding ~500 PMA parts a year and growing 18%, proving PMA demand and savings (HEICO CEO claims 25-35%, an old vendor claim).
ideas.wedge: 6 founding members with 30-80 aircraft (mostly 737NG/A320ceo) plus one lessor. The free hook is a private benchmark ("you paid 18% above pool median on 40 part numbers"), which creates the vendor conversation.
ideas.path_to_100m: Fee 2.5% (assumption within Premier's 1-3%) means $4B of managed spend. Mid-tier parts spend is ~$16-20B (40-50% of the $40B+ company claim, unverified), so $4B is 20-25%; adding component repair ($20B, Straits) and line services lifts the denominator to ~$30-35B and the share to ~12-13%. Heroic, but it is the only idea here whose revenue scales with volume without owning inventory.
ideas.who_does_it_today: SkySelect (AI procurement, 3,000+ suppliers, $9M raised Mar 2026), ePlane, PartsBase, Locatory and other marketplaces; AVIAA (business-aviation GPO only); airline-alliance joint purchasing; bilateral bulk deals like Satair-CASC; IATA's MRO SmartHub PMA tool; AJW and AAR as independent suppliers.
ideas.why_they_lose: Marketplaces automate search and RFQs but hold no pooled commitments or contracts; alliances are airline clubs with slow cycles; OEM-owned distributors cannot push PMA/USM against their parent's margin; nobody has the volume visibility to fund PMA offtake.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (volume improves terms, which attracts members), switching costs (rebates, embedded contracts) and a cross-airline price-history data asset.
ideas.earned_secret: Mid-tier airlines pay more not because of cost-to-serve but because of negotiating leverage, and PMA exists for a part only if someone can show developers committed volume. A pool can pre-commit offtake the way a hospital system commits volume (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit 6 founding members and sign data-sharing agreements; ingest 24 months of POs; deliver a private benchmark to each; run one 40-line pooled RFP; get a PMA developer to sign a non-binding offtake letter for 10 part numbers.

ideas.title: Graded Parts: authentication, escrow and indemnity for non-OEM parts
ideas.one_liner: An independent grade, escrowed settlement and an indemnity for used and non-OEM aircraft parts so a buyer can prove a part is what its paperwork says.
ideas.customer: Buyers of used serviceable material and distributor-sourced parts (airlines, MROs, lessors) plus the lenders and insurers who need a standard.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The buyer pays a protection fee (the Vinted flip), not the seller. Signer: VP Quality or Director of Materials; at lessors, Head of Technical. Lender and insurer mandates are the lever.
ideas.problem: AOG Technics forged at least 70 release certificates covering ~50 CFM56 parts (later reporting: 86 documents; unapproved parts on 126 engines), hitting Delta, United, Southwest, American and Virgin Australia; CFM is suing and the UK SFO charged a director. Used material is up to 30% of parts demand at some shops (Bain). Document exchanges verify paper, not parts, and nobody indemnifies the consequential cost (aircraft on ground, removing every part from that seller).
ideas.solution: Physical inspection by contracted Part 145 stations plus verification with the issuing organization, then a grade, escrow release on grade, and an indemnity underwritten by an aviation insurer. Start with CFM56/V2500 accessories and LLP stubs. Legal premise: the grader must not issue return-to-service documents unless it is a Part 145 holder, so inspection is subcontracted; indemnity needs an admitted insurer or MGA; escrow status needs checking (unverified).
ideas.why_now: Provenance became a board topic after AOG Technics; there is no FAA/EASA mandate for digital certificates (I searched), so demand has to come from buyers, lenders and insurers; the Aviation Supply Chain Integrity Coalition (Airbus, American, Boeing, Delta, GE Aerospace, United) focuses on prevention, leaving the grading and indemnity layer open.
ideas.wedge: CFM56-7B and V2500 accessories and LLP stubs from teardown houses. First 10 customers: 5 teardown sellers who want a premium for graded stock and 5 shops that buy USM heavily.
ideas.path_to_100m: Non-OEM-direct flows ~$20B (half of the $40B+ claim, unverified; USM alone $6.2B per the pool file). Fee: grade plus escrow 1.5% plus indemnity premium 1.0% = 2.5%, so $100M needs $4B of graded flows = ~20% of non-OEM-direct. Heroic: it only works if lenders, insurers and the airline coalition adopt the grade as the standard (the PSA path). If it cannot reach ~15% within five years it is dead.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Aeroxchange (digital 8130-3 exchange; Boeing/Southwest pilot); Dust Identity (publishes on 8130-3 fraud; product not verified); the Aviation Supply Chain Integrity Coalition; Honeywell GoDirect Trade and parts marketplaces (documents only); shops' own incoming inspection.
ideas.why_they_lose: Exchanges verify paper not parts; marketplaces earn from sellers and will not alienate them; the coalition prevents rather than underwrites; nobody holds inspection, escrow and underwriting together.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (independent grade standard plus claims history), branding (trust), network effects (sellers must be graded to reach buyers).
ideas.earned_secret: A Part 145 quality manager rejects a few percent of USM lots on paperwork alone and most are curable (insider hypothesis, unverified). The real cost of a fake is the aircraft on the ground and the regulator, so buyers will pay for indemnity against consequential removal if a neutral grade lets an insurer price it.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 2 Part 145 stations as graders; get a pilot indemnity term sheet from an aviation insurer; grade 500 lots from 10 sellers; show rejection and loss data to a lessor and a lender; meet the coalition.

ideas.title: Kit-First: induct the kit, not the engine
ideas.one_liner: Forecast a shop visit's missing parts 60-120 days ahead, assemble a documented kit, and induct the engine only when the kit is complete.
ideas.customer: Lessors and airlines facing 180-300 day turnarounds, and independent shops that buy kits.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Lessors (reserve claims, idle days) and airlines (cover-engine cost) pay for guaranteed turnaround; shops buy kits. Signer: Director of Engine Asset Management (lessor/airline) or VP Materials (shop).
ideas.problem: Touch time on a CFM56 overhaul is ~90-120 days (light ~45; V2500 60-70; GTF 260-365, per Acumen's indicative table) against real turnaround of 180-240 days, so 60-120 days are an engine waiting for parts. OEM parts demand exceeds supply by 10-20% (Bain). Shops are measured on stand utilization and paid time-and-material, so they induct on slot date and cannot gate induction; parts principals sell what they hold; lessors pay reserves but cannot direct workscope.
ideas.solution: A bill-of-materials forecast per engine, then a sourced kit (USM, PMA, repaired, new) supplied as customer-furnished material, with a contractual gate: the shop inducts only kit-complete and the customer gets a turnaround guarantee backed by a cover-engine option. Legal premise: customer-furnished material is normal in shop contracts (verify), every USM item needs traceability, and shops must accept third-party kits.
ideas.why_now: Parts shortage is the primary cause of slow turnaround (Bain); USM is up to 30% of shop parts demand; retirements feeding teardown are the only elastic source; JetCare claims 9-12 month OEM lead times (company claim).
ideas.wedge: CFM56-7B kits for lessor-owned engines going to independent shops. First 10 customers: three lessors and their two most-used shops.
ideas.path_to_100m: Principal materials business. Assumptions: 300 visits a year x $2.5M average kit = $750M revenue at 12-15% gross margin = $90-112M gross profit. Revenue crosses $100M at ~40 kitted visits, but the real test is $100M of gross profit, which needs ~300 visits (6% of narrowbody visits) and ~$120-150M of inventory capital (estimate). As a fee-only forecast layer it tops out near ~$20M, so the margin must come from materials.
ideas.who_does_it_today: AAR, AerSale, FTAI Aviation, HEICO/Wencor, StandardAero (own materials), JetCare, Stratton Aviation, AerFin, Aeras Aviation; unverified: CFM/GE customer material programs.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each principal sells its own stock and is rewarded for it; none forecasts the customer's whole bill of materials across channels; shops cannot adopt induction gating without losing utilization; the forecast needs findings data no single player shares.
ideas.moat: Process power plus a data-driven cornered resource (teardown-findings dataset), with counter-positioning against shops' utilization metrics. Weak unless the dataset becomes proprietary.
ideas.earned_secret: A planner knows by day 5 of teardown which 30-40 line items gate the visit (HPT blades, vanes, shrouds, LLP stubs) and most of them could be forecast months earlier from borescope and flight data (insider hypothesis, unverified). The delay is a supply-chain problem hidden inside a shop-floor metric.
